clues.revealExplanation: Honeyed words come off the tongue and a forked tongue is what a snake is trusted with; both describe sweet talk you should not believe.

blindReview.reason: A snake's forked tongue and a honeyed or honey-tongued speaker.

clues.wordAConnection: Honeyed charm is how a smooth talker works.
clues.wordBConnection: A snake charmer does the other kind.
clues.revealExplanation: A snake charmer does the charming and honeyed charm is how a smooth talker works.

blindReview.reason: Snake charmer is immediate; honey via honeyed, charming words, a figurative stretch.

clues.wordBConnection: A snake in the grass is what you find once you are in it.
clues.revealExplanation: A honeytrap is the lure and a snake in the grass is what you find once you are in it.

blindReview.reason: Honey trap is a set phrase; snake trap is not something players would reach for.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair; all three serve.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Literal shared property of both.

clues.revealExplanation: Trap: honey trap, spider's web.

blindReview.reason: Honey trap is a set phrase and a spider's web is a trap.

clues.revealExplanation: Fly: caught by honey, caught by the spider.

blindReview.reason: Spiders catch flies, and you catch more flies with honey than vinegar.

clues.revealExplanation: Sticky: honey, and the web.

blindReview.reason: Honey is sticky and so is a spider's web.

pairs.pairNote: A soft pair; POLLEN is the one hint that sits between both words, while BEE and BLOSSOM each face one of them.

clues.wordAConnection: Pollen is what bees carry home alongside the nectar.
clues.revealExplanation: Spring is pollen season and pollen is what bees carry home alongside the nectar.

blindReview.reason: Pollen season is spring; bees gathering pollen to make honey is how most people picture honey-making.

clues.revealExplanation: Bees come out in spring and the honey follows.

blindReview.reason: Bees make honey; bees being active in spring is seasonal background, not a link.

clues.wordAConnection: Blossom is the source of the nectar that becomes honey.
clues.revealExplanation: Spring blossom is the source of the nectar that becomes honey.

blindReview.reason: Spring blossom is direct; honey from blossoms (orange blossom honey) is a secondary association.

pairs.pairNote: Thin pair; GOLDEN carries it alone and SWEET is honey-only filler.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The only hint that reaches both words; golden honey and gold stars are both everyday images.

clues.revealExplanation: Golden: honey, and the star.

blindReview.reason: Honey is golden in colour and 'gold star' is a familiar phrase; a shared-property colour route like SWEET for APPLE+HONEY.

clues.revealExplanation: Sweet: honey, and the sweetheart star.

blindReview.reason: Honey is sweet (taste), but nothing about a star is sweet; the star side has no route.

pairs.pairNote: No PASS. Each hint is a one-sided compound; the pair needs a genuinely shared scene (e.g. a dining-car or a shared name) that neither hint supplies.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Neither hint reaches both words; CARGO at least admits honey as freight a train could carry, which BUN cannot do for train at all.

clues.revealExplanation: Cargo: honey on the train.

blindReview.reason: Trains carry cargo, but honey is not recognisably cargo to a player; train-only.

clues.revealExplanation: Bun: a honey bun for the ride.

blindReview.reason: Honey bun is a familiar compound/endearment, but there is no route from bun to train.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair; all three hints live in the same kitchen scene.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The most everyday scene: honey, lemon and hot water all meet in a cup of tea.

clues.revealExplanation: Lemon: honey lemon water.

blindReview.reason: Honey and lemon is a classic remedy pairing; lemon water is a familiar drink.

clues.revealExplanation: Tea: honey in hot water.

blindReview.reason: Honey is stirred into tea; tea is made with boiling water.

clues.revealExplanation: Dissolve: honey in water.

blindReview.reason: Honey dissolves in water: a verb route where honey is the thing dissolving and water the solvent.

pairs.pairNote: GINGERBREAD is the only workable hint; its honey side is moderate rather than immediate.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Reaches the witch through a universally known story and honey through a real, if secondary, ingredient link.

clues.revealExplanation: Gingerbread: the witch's house, honey-sweet.

blindReview.reason: The witch's gingerbread house in Hansel and Gretel is a famous scene; gingerbread is traditionally sweetened with honey (honey gingerbread/Lebkuchen), a moderate link.
Contains the target HONEY as a substring (rule failure) and has no route to witch anyway.

clues.revealExplanation: Potion: the witch's, with honey.

blindReview.reason: Witches brew potions, but honey as a potion ingredient is not a recognisable scene; witch-only.

pairs.pairNote: Both hints lean on honey compounds; BEAR has the better wolf side through shared forest/fairy-tale company.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Strong on honey and the most natural fellow-beast to wolf.

clues.wordBConnection: Bear and wolf in the forest.
clues.revealExplanation: Bear: honey eater, the wolf's neighbour.

blindReview.reason: Bears eat honey (Pooh, 'honey bear'); bear and wolf are the classic forest predators paired in fairy tales and The Jungle Book (Baloo and the wolf pack).

clues.wordBConnection: A badger, fierce as a wolf.
clues.revealExplanation: Badger: honey badger, wolf-fierce.

blindReview.reason: Honey badger is a familiar compound; badger to wolf is only 'another wild mammal', with no shared story or phrase.

pairs.pairNote: ICELANDIC would have been the best clue but breaks the substring rule.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The only legal hint reaching both; the horse-drawn sleigh on a frozen landscape is a shared winter scene.

clues.revealExplanation: Sleigh: horse-drawn, over the ice.

blindReview.reason: A one-horse open sleigh is a famous image; sleighs glide over snow and ice, a moderate ice link.
Icelandic horse is a real breed, but the hint contains the target ICE as a substring, a rule failure.

clues.wordAConnection: Sven pulls the sled like a horse.
clues.revealExplanation: Frozen: ice, and the sled-puller.

blindReview.reason: Ice is frozen water; the only horse route is the water-horse Nokk in Frozen II, which is niche and needs explaining.

pairs.pairNote: SMITH is the one defensible hint; SHOE is horse-only and TRAIN needs the 'iron horse' nickname.

clues.wordBConnection: And works the iron to do it.
clues.revealExplanation: The blacksmith works iron and shoes the horses.

blindReview.reason: A blacksmith works iron and the classic image is of him shoeing a horse.

clues.wordAConnection: A horseshoe is what gets nailed on.
clues.wordBConnection: And it is a bent bar of iron.
clues.revealExplanation: A horseshoe is a bent bar of iron.

blindReview.reason: Horseshoe is an immediate compound; there is no 'shoe + iron' compound, so iron is only reached by recalling the material.

clues.wordAConnection: The iron horse was what they called the steam train when it first appeared.
clues.wordBConnection: And it was built of iron.
clues.revealExplanation: The iron horse was what they called the steam train when it first appeared.

blindReview.reason: Both sides depend on knowing the nickname 'iron horse' for a locomotive, and TRAIN itself is not part of that compound.

pairs.pairNote: BOLT is a genuine two-way clue; its key side goes through the lock rather than the key itself.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Neat double meaning: the bolting horse and the bolt a key throws.

clues.wordAConnection: A horse bolts across the field.
clues.wordBConnection: A bolt is also the lock a key throws.
clues.revealExplanation: A horse bolts across the field and a bolt is the lock a key throws.

blindReview.reason: A horse bolts (verb); a key turns the bolt of a lock (deadbolt), a lock-hardware route to key.

clues.wordAConnection: The stable door is the horse's.
clues.wordBConnection: Locking it after the horse has bolted is the proverb: the key comes too late.
clues.revealExplanation: Locking the stable door after the horse has bolted is the proverb about acting too late.

blindReview.reason: Horses live in stables; there is no recognisable route from stable to key (the proverb about the stable door is about the horse, not a key).

pairs.pairNote: Rich pair; KINGDOM is lost only to the substring rule.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: One rhyme everyone knows that literally contains the king's horses.

clues.revealExplanation: Humpty Dumpty: the king's horses.

blindReview.reason: 'All the king's horses and all the king's men' in Humpty Dumpty names both words in one nursery rhyme.

clues.revealExplanation: Knight: the king's rider.

blindReview.reason: A knight rides a horse and serves a king; in chess the knight is the horse piece beside the king.

clues.revealExplanation: Richard: the king who'd trade his kingdom for a horse.

blindReview.reason: King Richard (Lionheart, Richard III) is a familiar royal name; the horse comes from Richard III's 'my kingdom for a horse', which many but not all players will have met.
'My kingdom for a horse' is a fine route, but the hint contains the target KING as a substring, a rule failure.

pairs.pairNote: Every hint passes; STEED is flagged as a near-synonym of HORSE for the owner's judgement.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The most vivid single scene containing both a knight and a horse.

clues.revealExplanation: Joust: knights on horses.

blindReview.reason: Knights joust on horseback; one scene holds both words.

clues.revealExplanation: Steed: the knight's horse.

blindReview.reason: A steed is a horse (near-synonym) and 'the knight's steed' is a stock phrase; passes but gives the horse away almost directly.

clues.revealExplanation: Chess: the knight is the horse.

blindReview.reason: The chess knight is shaped like, and often called, the horse.

clues.revealExplanation: Armor: knight and horse.

blindReview.reason: Knights wear armour; warhorses in tournaments are armoured too (barding), a recognisable if secondary image.

pairs.pairNote: Solid pair with three different routes.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Compound on one side, antonym on the other; both instant.

clues.wordAConnection: A dark horse is the unexpected winner.
clues.wordBConnection: Dark is the opposite of light.
clues.revealExplanation: A dark horse is the unexpected winner and dark is the opposite of light.

blindReview.reason: 'Dark horse' is a common compound and dark is the opposite of light.

clues.wordAConnection: Light horse is the historical name for light cavalry.
clues.wordBConnection: Light is the word that does the work in the name.
clues.revealExplanation: Light horse is the historical name for light cavalry.

blindReview.reason: Cavalry are horse soldiers; 'light cavalry' / the Light Brigade is a familiar military phrase.

clues.wordAConnection: A horse is judged on nothing but speed.
clues.wordBConnection: Light travels at the fastest speed there is.
clues.revealExplanation: Light travels at the fastest speed there is and a horse is judged on nothing but speed.

blindReview.reason: Speed of light is a fixed phrase; horses are the archetypal fast animal (racing, galloping), a shared-property route.

pairs.pairNote: MANE is excellent; CAROUSEL's lion side is real but weak.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The one physical feature these two animals uniquely share.

clues.revealExplanation: Mane: horse and lion.

blindReview.reason: Both the horse and the lion are the animals famous for a mane; a textbook shared property.

clues.revealExplanation: Narnia: the lion, and the horse.

blindReview.reason: Aslan the lion is Narnia's centrepiece; Narnia's talking horses (The Horse and His Boy, Bree) are a real but secondary element.

clues.revealExplanation: Carousel: horses, and a lion to ride.

blindReview.reason: Carousel horses are iconic; lions appear on menagerie carousels but a player is unlikely to reach lion from carousel without prompting.

pairs.pairNote: No PASS. MARE is a clever clue for astronomy-literate players but too specialist to pass outright.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The only hint with a factual route to both words, though the lunar 'mare' is niche knowledge.

clues.wordAConnection: A mare is a female horse.
clues.wordBConnection: The dark plains on the moon are called maria, from the same word.
clues.revealExplanation: A mare is a female horse, and the dark plains on the moon are called maria, from mare.

blindReview.reason: A mare is a female horse; the moon's dark plains are the lunar maria (Mare Tranquillitatis), a correct but specialist route.

clues.wordAConnection: A horseshoe is the crescent nailed on.
clues.wordBConnection: Which is exactly the shape of the moon in its thin phase.
clues.revealExplanation: A horseshoe is a crescent, which is exactly the shape of the moon in its thin phase.

blindReview.reason: Horseshoe is immediate, but the moon side exists only as a crescent-shape resemblance that no player would reach unprompted.

pairs.pairNote: CINDERELLA is excellent; the other two are soft stable/mood associations.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The mice-into-horses transformation is one of the best-known scenes in any fairy tale.

clues.revealExplanation: Cinderella: mice into horses.

blindReview.reason: In Cinderella the fairy godmother turns the mice into horses; one story holds both.

clues.revealExplanation: Stable: horses, and mice in the straw.

blindReview.reason: Horse stable is immediate; mice living among the hay and grain of a stable is plausible but not a scene players reach readily.

clues.revealExplanation: Scared: the horse, of a mouse.

blindReview.reason: Horses are famously skittish and the mouse is the byword for timidity, but neither side is more than a mood association.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair; MARE is the standout.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Direct horse word that also completes NIGHTMARE.

clues.wordAConnection: A mare is a female horse.
clues.revealExplanation: Mare: a horse, and the night-mare.

blindReview.reason: A mare is a female horse and night+mare makes nightmare, a compound route.

clues.revealExplanation: Revere: the midnight ride.

blindReview.reason: Paul Revere's midnight ride was on horseback through the night; US-centric but widely taught.

clues.revealExplanation: Headless: the horseman of the night.

blindReview.reason: The Headless Horseman rides a horse and haunts Sleepy Hollow by night.

pairs.pairNote: SEA is the legal form of the seahorse idea; POSEIDON is a good second for mythology-aware players.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Does everything SEAHORSE wanted to do without containing the target.

clues.revealExplanation: Sea: the ocean, and the seahorse.

blindReview.reason: Sea is a near-synonym of ocean and sea+horse makes seahorse; a legal compound route that SEAHORSE itself breaks.
Contains the target HORSE as a substring, a rule failure despite reaching both.

clues.revealExplanation: Poseidon: god of ocean and horses.

blindReview.reason: Poseidon is god of the sea; he is also god of horses who created them and drives a horse-drawn chariot, a true but mythology-buff route.

clues.revealExplanation: Waves: the ocean's white horses.

blindReview.reason: Ocean waves are immediate; the horse side rests on the poetic 'white horses' for breakers, which most players will not reach.

pairs.pairNote: SEA is strong; HIGHWAYMAN is a thoughtful category route; BUCCANEER is pirate-only.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Immediate on both sides through the pirate's element and the seahorse compound.

clues.revealExplanation: Sea: seahorse, sea pirate.

blindReview.reason: Pirates sail the sea; sea+horse makes seahorse.

clues.wordBConnection: A highwayman is a land pirate.
clues.revealExplanation: Highwayman: the pirate of the road, on horseback.

blindReview.reason: A highwayman robs from horseback; he is the land-robber counterpart of the pirate, a shared outlaw category players recognise.

clues.wordAConnection: The Broncos' horse, rivals of the Buccaneers.
clues.revealExplanation: Buccaneer: pirate, and a football name like Bronco.

blindReview.reason: Buccaneer is simply a pirate; nothing points to horse.

pairs.pairNote: Good pair; ASCOT and RACES share the racing route.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: A single image, the horse-drawn royal carriage, contains both words.

clues.revealExplanation: Carriage: the Queen's, drawn by horses.

blindReview.reason: Carriages are horse-drawn and the Queen rides in the royal carriage on state occasions.

clues.revealExplanation: Ascot: the Queen's race day.

blindReview.reason: Royal Ascot is the horse-racing meeting the Queen famously attended each year; well known beyond Britain through the royal link.

clues.revealExplanation: Races: the Queen's horses.

blindReview.reason: Horse races are immediate; the Queen's love of the races is widely known, though a step removed.

pairs.pairNote: All three pass; SHOW's ring side is the softest.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Ring and horse are both stock parts of the circus picture.

clues.revealExplanation: Circus: horses in the ring.

blindReview.reason: The circus ring and the circus horse act are both classic circus images.

clues.revealExplanation: Arena: the horse's ring.

blindReview.reason: Horses are ridden in a riding arena; a ring (boxing, circus) is an arena, a near-synonym.

clues.revealExplanation: Show: horses in the ring.

blindReview.reason: Horse show is a familiar compound; the 'show ring' is where show horses are judged, a moderate ring link.

pairs.pairNote: Hard pair; WESTWORLD is pop-culture dependent and MECHANICAL's horse side is modest.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Horses and robots are the two defining ingredients of the franchise.

clues.revealExplanation: Westworld: robots on horseback.

blindReview.reason: Westworld is a Western theme park (horses) populated by robot hosts; one title holds both for anyone who knows it.

clues.revealExplanation: Mechanical: horse or robot.

blindReview.reason: Robots are mechanical; the coin-operated mechanical horse ride is a familiar object.

clues.revealExplanation: Bull: the robot you ride like a horse.

blindReview.reason: Bull reaches horse only as a fellow rodeo/ranch animal and robot only via the 'mechanical bull' ride; neither route is clear enough to count.

pairs.pairNote: No PASS. The obvious clue (rocking horse) is forbidden by the substring rule; the pair needs a replacement such as a shared name or 'pet'.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The only legal hint with any route to rock; ROCKING is the better clue but breaks the substring rule.

blindReview.reason: Rocking horse is a perfect compound, but ROCKING contains the target ROCK as a substring, a rule failure.

clues.revealExplanation: Crazy Horse, carved in rock.

blindReview.reason: Crazy Horse is a famous name (Lakota leader, memorial); the rock side is only via Neil Young's band Crazy Horse being a rock act, which itself goes through 'horse'.

clues.revealExplanation: Shoe: the horse's, on the rocks.

blindReview.reason: Horseshoe is immediate; nothing connects shoe to rock.

pairs.pairNote: WAR works; DERBY and BLANKET both lean on the same obscure Kentucky Derby rose tradition.

clues.revealExplanation: A warhorse; the Wars of the Roses.

blindReview.reason: War horse is a stock phrase and the War(s) of the Roses is well known from history and the film title.

clues.wordAConnection: The Kentucky Derby is a horse race.
clues.wordBConnection: It is known as the Run for the Roses.
clues.revealExplanation: The Kentucky Derby is a horse race known as the Run for the Roses.

blindReview.reason: Derby is a horse race; the Kentucky Derby's 'Run for the Roses' is a detail only fans know.

clues.wordAConnection: The winning horse is draped in one.
clues.wordBConnection: And it is woven out of roses.
clues.revealExplanation: The winning horse is draped in a blanket of roses.

blindReview.reason: Horse blanket is fine, but the Derby's 'blanket of roses' is trivia a stranger will not reach.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair across three routes.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The salt lick is a single object that belongs to horses.

clues.revealExplanation: A worked horse sweats and dries white with salt.

blindReview.reason: Horses visibly sweat (lathered) and sweat is salty; a shared-property route.

clues.wordAConnection: The block is put out in the field for horses.
clues.revealExplanation: A salt lick is the block put out in the field for horses.

blindReview.reason: A salt lick is the block horses and livestock lick; one object holds both.

clues.wordAConnection: You can lead a horse to water but not make it drink.
clues.wordBConnection: Salt water is the kind nothing can drink.
clues.revealExplanation: You can lead a horse to water but not make it drink, and salt water is the kind nothing can drink.

blindReview.reason: Lead a horse to water; salt water is a fixed compound.

pairs.pairNote: No PASS. Both live hints describe the same 'horse spooked by a shadow' scene, in which shadow is only the cause.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Reaches horse directly and gives shadow two half-routes (the thing that spooks a horse; a spectral figure).

clues.wordAConnection: A horse shies on the road.
clues.revealExplanation: A horse shies at its own shadow on the road.

blindReview.reason: A horse shies (verb) and horses famously shy at shadows, but shadow is reached only as the thing shied at.

clues.wordAConnection: A horse is what gets spooked.
clues.wordBConnection: And a shadow is exactly what does it.
clues.revealExplanation: A shadow is exactly what spooks a horse.

blindReview.reason: A horse spooks (verb), typically at a shadow, and a spook is a ghostly shadowy figure; same scene as SHY with a slightly better shadow side.

clues.wordAConnection: The rider sits on the horse.
clues.wordBConnection: And his shadow is thrown along the ground beside it.
clues.revealExplanation: The rider's shadow is thrown along the ground beside the horse.

blindReview.reason: Horse rider is immediate; 'Shadow Riders' is an obscure novel/film and gives shadow no recognisable route.

pairs.pairNote: Both pass; TEETH is the more playful shared property.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The seahorse compound makes the horse side as fast as the shark side.

clues.revealExplanation: Sea: seahorse, and shark.

blindReview.reason: Sharks live in the sea; sea+horse makes seahorse.

clues.revealExplanation: Teeth: horse and shark.

blindReview.reason: Shark teeth are iconic; horse teeth are a well-known feature too (gift horse in the mouth, 'long in the tooth', horse-toothed grin).

pairs.pairNote: Good pair; REAR is a nice shared verb.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Instant on both sides with a compound and a phrase to help.

clues.wordBConnection: A snake in the grass is what you never see coming.
clues.revealExplanation: A horse lives on grass and a snake in the grass is what you never see coming.

blindReview.reason: Horses graze on grass; grass snake is a familiar compound (and 'snake in the grass' a stock phrase).

clues.revealExplanation: A startled horse rears up and so does a cobra.

blindReview.reason: A horse rears up on its hind legs; a cobra rears up to strike, the same verb on both sides.

pairs.pairNote: Both pass; FLY is the stronger.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Compound on one side, the spider's prey on the other.

clues.revealExplanation: Fly: horse fly, spider's meal.

blindReview.reason: Horsefly is a compound; spiders catch flies in their webs.

clues.revealExplanation: Barn: horses, and spiders in the rafters.

blindReview.reason: Horses are kept in barns; the barn spider is a real species and Charlotte of Charlotte's Web is one, spinning her web in a barn.

pairs.pairNote: JUMP is excellent; DERBY's spring side is calendar knowledge.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Verb route that is immediate on both sides.

clues.revealExplanation: A horse jumps the fence and to spring is to jump.

blindReview.reason: Horses jump (show jumping); to spring is to jump, a verb synonym.

clues.wordAConnection: A foal is a young horse.
clues.wordBConnection: And they are born in spring.
clues.revealExplanation: Foals are born in spring.

blindReview.reason: A foal is a baby horse; foals, like lambs, are born in spring, a familiar seasonal scene.

clues.wordAConnection: The Derby is the great horse race.
clues.wordBConnection: And it is run in spring.
clues.revealExplanation: The Derby is the great horse race and it is run in spring.

blindReview.reason: The Derby is a famous horse race; its spring timing (Kentucky Derby in May) is known to racing followers but not a route most players would take.

pairs.pairNote: PEGASUS carries the pair; BLAZE is a decent horsey double meaning that needs equestrian knowledge.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: A horse that is literally among the stars.

clues.revealExplanation: Pegasus: the horse in the stars.

blindReview.reason: Pegasus is the winged horse of myth and a well-known constellation.

clues.wordBConnection: A star marking is a small blaze.
clues.revealExplanation: Blaze: the horse's forehead star.

blindReview.reason: Blaze is a white facial marking and classic horse name, and stars blaze ('blazing star'); both routes are real but each is a step removed.

clues.revealExplanation: Trigger: the horse who was a star.

blindReview.reason: Trigger was Roy Rogers' horse, a dated reference, and star is reached only by calling Trigger a movie-star horse.

pairs.pairNote: TRACK is the real bridge; IRON is a clever period phrase that needs explaining.

clues.revealExplanation: Race track, train track.

blindReview.reason: Train tracks and the horse race track.
Iron horse is an old nickname for a train, but neither side is reached without knowing that phrase.
Train station is direct; no horse link.
Horse saddle is direct; no train link.

pairs.pairNote: Very strong pair.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The proverb everybody knows, and LEAD is the word that triggers it.

clues.revealExplanation: Lead a horse to water.

blindReview.reason: 'You can lead a horse to water' names both words in one proverb.

clues.revealExplanation: Drink: the horse at the water.

blindReview.reason: '...but you can't make it drink' completes the same proverb; water is what is drunk.

clues.revealExplanation: Trough: water for the horse.

blindReview.reason: A water trough is where horses drink; one object holds both.

pairs.pairNote: RIDE is the only two-way hint; HAG and BROOM are witch-only.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The one thing a horse and a witch's broom have in common, expressed as a verb.

clues.revealExplanation: Ride: horse, or broom.

blindReview.reason: You ride a horse and a witch rides her broom; a shared verb.

clues.wordAConnection: Hag rhymes with nag, an old horse.
clues.revealExplanation: Hag: the witch, and the nag.

blindReview.reason: Hag is a witch synonym; there is no route to horse (the worn-out horse is a 'nag', not a hag).

clues.revealExplanation: Broom: the witch's ride, and the hobby horse.

blindReview.reason: Witches ride brooms; a horse has no recognisable link to a broom beyond the fact that both are ridden.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair; PACK is the cleanest.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Two compounds, one word.

clues.revealExplanation: Wild: horse and wolf.

blindReview.reason: Wild horse is a compound (mustangs) and the wolf is the archetypal wild animal.

clues.revealExplanation: Pack: horse, or wolf.

blindReview.reason: Wolf pack and packhorse are both everyday compounds.

clues.revealExplanation: Prey: the horse, to the wolf.

blindReview.reason: Wolves hunt prey; horses are classic prey animals, and wolves hunting horses is the relation between the two.

pairs.pairNote: AGE is excellent; the other two are ice-first with weak iron sides.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Parallel compounds that land both words instantly.

clues.revealExplanation: Age: Ice Age, Iron Age.

blindReview.reason: Ice Age and Iron Age are both familiar compounds.

clues.revealExplanation: Skates: ice, on iron blades.

blindReview.reason: Ice skates are immediate; iron is reached only as the metal of the blade, which few players would name.

clues.revealExplanation: Cold: ice, and iron.

blindReview.reason: Ice is cold; 'cold iron' is a folklore phrase and iron feels cold to the touch, but the iron side is a soft property link.

pairs.pairNote: No PASS. The pair wants a shared compound (e.g. a word that pairs with both) which neither hint supplies.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Immediate on key and gives ice the frozen-lock scene; the only hint with any two-way reach.

clues.revealExplanation: Lock: for the key, frozen shut.

blindReview.reason: Lock and key are inseparable; ice is reached only through a frozen lock in winter (de-icer) or 'ice-locked', a seasonal scene rather than a firm link.

clues.wordBConnection: A key frozen in the lock.
clues.revealExplanation: Frozen: ice, and the stuck key.

blindReview.reason: Ice is frozen; a key is not frozen in any familiar sense (a stuck keyboard key is 'frozen' only loosely).

pairs.pairNote: Two moderate passes, each strong on one side and fair on the other; ELVIS is king-only.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Direct on ice with a traditional personified-king route.

clues.revealExplanation: Night: the Night King of the ice.

blindReview.reason: The Night King of Game of Thrones is the lord of the ice-bound White Walkers; the single reference reaches king directly and ice through the character's nature, with cold nights as a fallback.

clues.revealExplanation: Frost: the ice king.

blindReview.reason: Frost is ice crystals; 'the Frost King' / Jack Frost is a familiar winter-folklore figure, a moderate king link.

clues.revealExplanation: Elvis: the King, on ice.

blindReview.reason: Elvis is 'the King'; nothing links Elvis to ice.

pairs.pairNote: WHITE holds the pair on a colour route; ARMOR is knight-only.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Phrase on the knight side, colour on the ice side; the only hint that reaches both.

clues.wordAConnection: The White Walkers of the ice.
clues.revealExplanation: White: knight, and the ice walkers.

blindReview.reason: 'White knight' is a fixed phrase; ice and snow are the white of winter, a shared-colour route like GOLDEN for honey.

clues.revealExplanation: Armor: the knight's, and ice.

blindReview.reason: Knights wear armour; ice as armour exists only in video games and is not a recognisable route.

pairs.pairNote: Two good passes; GLACIER is ice-only filler.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: What ice does and what light does, in one word.

clues.revealExplanation: Sparkle: light on ice.

blindReview.reason: Ice sparkles and sparkle is a quality of light; a shared-property verb.

clues.revealExplanation: Northern: lights over the ice.

blindReview.reason: Northern Lights is a fixed compound; the frozen north (Arctic ice) gives ice a recognisable geographic route.

clues.revealExplanation: Glacier: ice that glows.

blindReview.reason: A glacier is a river of ice; there is no route to light.

pairs.pairNote: Both passes come from the same story; AGE presumes a lion that is not in the film.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Names the frozen world rather than just its lion, so ice and lion are equally reachable.

clues.revealExplanation: Narnia: the lion, and the ice.

blindReview.reason: Narnia is the land of eternal winter ruled over by ice until Aslan the lion returns; both words are central to the story.

clues.revealExplanation: Aslan: the lion who ended the ice.

blindReview.reason: Aslan is Narnia's lion; he ends the White Witch's endless winter, so the ice side comes through the frozen Narnia he thaws.

clues.wordBConnection: Diego, the Ice Age big cat.
clues.revealExplanation: Age: Ice Age, with its big cat.

blindReview.reason: Ice Age is immediate, but the Ice Age films feature a sabre-toothed cat (Diego), not a lion, and no other route to lion exists.

pairs.pairNote: EUROPA carries the pair; FROZEN and WINTER are ice-first.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: A real icy moon; the only hint with a firm route to both.

clues.revealExplanation: Europa: the ice moon.

blindReview.reason: Europa is Jupiter's ice-covered moon; a correct single reference reaching both for anyone with basic astronomy.

clues.revealExplanation: Winter: ice under the moon.

blindReview.reason: Winter brings ice; 'winter moon' / the Cold Moon is a real but soft seasonal association.

clues.revealExplanation: Frozen: ice, and the moon.

blindReview.reason: Ice is frozen; the moon is not recognisably 'frozen' to a player without the icy-moon astronomy EUROPA already carries.

pairs.pairNote: Hard pair; FROZEN's mouse side is the computer sense and should be judged on whether the owner accepts that reading.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: The frozen computer mouse makes this the only hint that reaches both words.

clues.revealExplanation: Frozen: Disney's ice.

blindReview.reason: Ice is frozen water; 'my mouse is frozen' is a familiar computer complaint, giving mouse a genuine everyday route.

clues.revealExplanation: Freezer: ice, and frozen mice.

blindReview.reason: Ice lives in the freezer; mouse has no recognisable freezer route.

pairs.pairNote: All pass; FROST is the natural choice.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: Ice that appears in the night; immediate on both.

clues.revealExplanation: Frost: ice, overnight.

blindReview.reason: Frost is ice crystals and forms overnight ('frost tonight'); a familiar weather scene.

clues.revealExplanation: Freeze: ice by night.

blindReview.reason: Freezing makes ice; forecasts warn of an overnight freeze, so night is the time temperatures drop below freezing.

clues.revealExplanation: King: the Night King of ice.

blindReview.reason: The Night King (Game of Thrones) is a familiar compound; Ice King (Adventure Time) and the Night King's icy nature give ice a moderate route.

pairs.pairNote: Strong pair; ICEBERG fails only on the substring rule.

reviewerBestAvailable.why: One story everyone knows, with ice and ocean as its two protagonists.

clues.revealExplanation: Arctic: the ice ocean.

blindReview.reason: Arctic ice and the Arctic Ocean; a geographic route landing both.

clues.revealExplanation: Titanic: ice in the ocean.

blindReview.reason: The Titanic struck an iceberg and sank in the ocean; a universally known story holding both.

clues.revealExplanation: Floe: ice on the ocean.

blindReview.reason: An ice floe is a sheet of floating ice drifting on the ocean; the word is slightly uncommon but tied only to this scene.
Contains the target ICE as a substring, a rule failure despite the obvious ocean route.

pairs.pairNote: ELSA and FROZEN are both clean (one film); SNOW passes via the Snow Queen title; ARENDELLE is correct but moderate recognizability; CHESS and CUBE are one-sided.

clues.wordBConnection: Elsa is the queen of Arendelle.
clues.revealExplanation: Elsa, Frozen's ice queen.

blindReview.reason: Elsa from Frozen has ice magic and is crowned Queen of Arendelle; a household name.

clues.wordBConnection: Frozen, the film about Queen Elsa.
clues.revealExplanation: Frozen: ice, and the film about a queen.

blindReview.reason: Frozen is the plain state of ice and the Disney film whose heroine becomes queen; the film is broadly known.

clues.revealExplanation: The Snow Queen.

blindReview.reason: Snow sits next to ice; 'Snow Queen' (Andersen, Narnia, Frozen's source) is a known title, a solid second reach.
Arendelle is the kingdom in Frozen ruled by the ice-powered Queen Elsa; accurate, but the name is known mainly to Frozen fans and parents.

provenance.authorReason: generic: ICE only, and fits half the board

blindReview.reason: Cold is the property of ice; the 'ice queen' idiom for an aloof woman is the only route to QUEEN, and that route goes through the other target rather than a 'cold queen' compound.
The queen is a chess piece; chess has no ice sense.
Ice cube is direct; nothing regal about a cube.

pairs.pairNote: CAST is the elegant double meaning and HEAVY the sturdy antonym; GLOW is light-only.

clues.wordAConnection: Iron is the byword for heavy.

blindReview.reason: Iron is heavy and heavy is the opposite of light.

clues.wordBConnection: Light is cast across a room.
clues.revealExplanation: Cast iron is the material and light is cast across a room.

blindReview.reason: Cast iron and cast light are both standard collocations.

clues.wordBConnection: Which is light coming straight out of the metal.
clues.revealExplanation: Iron glows when it is heated, which is light coming straight out of the metal.

blindReview.reason: Light glows; hot iron glowing is true but needs the player to picture a forge.

pairs.pairNote: MAP is a neat double meaning and PRESS a good plain-sense hint; GARDEN is rose-only.

clues.wordAConnection: Every map carries a key to read it by.
clues.wordBConnection: And a compass rose to point it north.
clues.revealExplanation: Every map carries a key to read it by and a compass rose to point it north.

blindReview.reason: A map has a key (legend) and a compass rose; both are standard map vocabulary.

clues.wordBConnection: You press a rose flat between the pages of a book.
clues.revealExplanation: You press a key and you press a rose flat between the pages of a book.

blindReview.reason: You press a key, and pressing a rose in a book is a familiar keepsake practice.

clues.wordAConnection: In The Secret Garden a buried key unlocks the door.
clues.wordBConnection: And the walled garden behind it is full of roses.
clues.revealExplanation: In The Secret Garden a buried key unlocks the walled garden full of roses.

blindReview.reason: Rose garden is direct, but nothing leads from garden to key short of The Secret Garden's locked door.

pairs.pairNote: WIND is the one hint that reaches both words from a single wind-up image; CLOCK is the same idea one step further away.

clues.wordAConnection: You wind it using a key.
clues.wordBConnection: And what you are winding is a clockwork spring.
clues.revealExplanation: You wind a clockwork spring using a key.

blindReview.reason: You wind a clock or toy with a key, which tightens its spring; spring breezes give a second route.

clues.wordAConnection: A key is what releases it.
clues.wordBConnection: A lock is a spring-loaded mechanism.
clues.revealExplanation: A lock is a spring-loaded mechanism and a key is what releases it.

blindReview.reason: Lock and key is immediate; a spring-loaded lock is mechanical detail.

clues.wordAConnection: A clock is wound with a key.
clues.revealExplanation: A clock is driven by a spring and wound with a key.

blindReview.reason: A wind-up clock has a key and a mainspring, but neither is the first thing a player thinks of for clock.

pairs.pairNote: MUFASA and SIMBA are both clean (same film); JUNGLE rides one universal idiom; THRONE and CROWN are king-side words with only a heraldic reach to the lion.

clues.wordAConnection: Mufasa is the king of the Pride Lands.
clues.revealExplanation: Mufasa, the lion king in The Lion King.

blindReview.reason: Mufasa is the reigning king in The Lion King and is a lion; both sides are immediate for anyone who knows the film.

clues.wordAConnection: Simba grows up to be king.
clues.revealExplanation: Simba, the lion who becomes king in The Lion King.

blindReview.reason: Simba is the lion cub who becomes king in The Lion King; the film title itself carries both words.

clues.revealExplanation: The lion is the king of the jungle.

blindReview.reason: The stock phrase 'king of the jungle' names the lion; KING is reached through that same idiom, which is universal.

provenance.authorReason: reaches KING only; Pride Rock is a stretch

blindReview.reason: A throne is a king's seat; lions reach it only via heraldry or Pride Rock in The Lion King, which needs explaining.

provenance.authorReason: KING only; also a board word that would be a target elsewhere

blindReview.reason: Crown is the king's emblem; the crowned heraldic lion (as on the English royal arms) is a stretch for most players.

clues.revealExplanation: Aslan the lion is the king of Narnia.

blindReview.reason: Aslan the lion is Narnia's best-known figure via 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe'; KING requires knowing Aslan rules Narnia or that the children become kings and queens.
A mane is the lion's defining feature; nothing about it points to a king.
Lions roar; kings do not, and no idiom or compound bridges the gap.

pairs.pairNote: ELVIS is the clean two-way hit; BETHLEHEM works via the nativity story.

clues.revealExplanation: Elvis: the King, and a star.

blindReview.reason: Elvis is The King and a rock star.

clues.wordAConnection: The three kings came to Bethlehem.
clues.revealExplanation: The Star of Bethlehem and the three kings who followed it.

blindReview.reason: The Star of Bethlehem led the three kings to the newborn King.
Kings are royal; stars are not.
Stars have fame; kings are not defined by it.

pairs.pairNote: DARK and BLACK both work through a famous Knight compound plus a plain night sense; MARE passes on the nightmare compound; ARMOR and OWL are one-sided.

clues.revealExplanation: The Black Knight; a black night.

blindReview.reason: Judged as compounds: 'Black Knight' (Arthurian legend, Monty Python, the Marvel character) on one side and 'black as night' / 'black night' on the other; both are established phrases.

clues.revealExplanation: The Dark Knight, and a dark night.

blindReview.reason: Dark is the plain property of night, and 'The Dark Knight' (Batman) is a household title.

clues.revealExplanation: A knight's mare, and a nightmare.

blindReview.reason: Night + mare makes nightmare; a mare is a horse, the knight's mount and the shape of the chess knight, so KNIGHT is a solid second reach.

provenance.authorReason: knight in shining armour reaches KNIGHT only

blindReview.reason: 'Knight in shining armor' is immediate; stars shining at night is a soft reach and 'shining night' is not a compound.
Armor is knight equipment with no night sense.
Owls are the nocturnal emblem of night; nothing links them to knights.

pairs.pairNote: CAST is the elegant answer and DARK the blunt one; PUPPET and SUN lean on the shadow or light side respectively.

clues.wordBConnection: And the thing cast is a shadow.
clues.revealExplanation: Light is what casts a shadow.

blindReview.reason: You cast a shadow and cast light on something; both collocations are everyday.

clues.wordAConnection: Dark is what light is not.
clues.wordBConnection: A shadow is a patch of it.
clues.revealExplanation: A shadow is a patch of dark and dark is what light is not.

blindReview.reason: Dark is the direct opposite of light and the substance of a shadow; generic but natural to both.

clues.wordAConnection: Shadow puppets need a lamp behind them.
clues.wordBConnection: And what reaches the screen is nothing but shadow.
clues.revealExplanation: Shadow puppets work by putting a hand between a lamp and the screen.

blindReview.reason: Shadow puppet is direct; the lamp behind the puppet is a second step most players will not make unprompted.

clues.wordBConnection: And it is what puts shadows on the ground.
clues.revealExplanation: The sun is the light that puts shadows on the ground.

blindReview.reason: Sunlight is immediate; sun to shadow requires thinking about what the sun produces behind an object.

pairs.pairNote: WARDROBE is the perfect title hint; NARNIA is the same reference a step wider.

clues.revealExplanation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

reference.source: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

blindReview.reason: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe names both words in its title.

clues.revealExplanation: Narnia: the Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

blindReview.reason: Narnia's story centres on the lion Aslan and the White Witch.
Aslan is the lion; the White Witch is his enemy but one step removed.
Lions roar; witches cackle.

pairs.pairNote: TIDE is excellent and BLUE is a natural colour hint for both; PULL is the tide idea without the word; the rest are one-sided.

clues.revealExplanation: A blue moon over the blue ocean.

provenance.authorReason: blue moon is a phrase, blue ocean is a colour: generic colour clue

blindReview.reason: 'Blue moon' is a common idiom and the ocean is the archetypal blue thing; both sides are direct.

clues.wordAConnection: The moon's pull makes the tide.
clues.revealExplanation: The moon pulls the ocean's tides.

blindReview.reason: Tides belong to the ocean and are commonly known to be caused by the moon.
The moon's gravitational pull drives the ocean's tides, but both words need that explanation; PULL alone is abstract.
Ocean floor is a set phrase; 'moon floor' is not.
'The deep' is the ocean; the moon is not described as deep.
Craters are the moon's surface feature; no ocean sense.

pairs.pairNote: SKY is plain but natural to both; nothing else reaches the moon.

clues.revealExplanation: Both hang in the night sky.

blindReview.reason: Moon and stars are both in the night sky.

clues.revealExplanation: The crescent moon, as in the star and crescent.

blindReview.reason: Crescent moon is direct; star only via the crescent-and-star emblem.
Twinkle twinkle little star; the moon does not twinkle.
Wish upon a star is direct; no wishing on the moon.

pairs.pairNote: HOWL is the clean two-way hint and NIGHT is a natural shared setting; CRY and FULL each lean on one side; PACK is wolf-only.

clues.revealExplanation: A wolf howls at the moon.

blindReview.reason: Wolves howl, and 'howl at the moon' is a stock phrase.

clues.wordBConnection: The wolf is a creature of the night.
clues.revealExplanation: Both belong to the night.

blindReview.reason: The moon belongs to the night, and the wolf is culturally a creature of the night (howling in the dark, werewolf lore); natural to both.

provenance.authorReason: weaker form of HOWL and one-sided

clues.wordBConnection: The werewolf of the full moon.
clues.revealExplanation: The full moon that makes the werewolf.

blindReview.reason: The Caribbean Sea and Pirates of the Caribbean.

blindReview.reason: Ships sail the ocean and pirate ship is a compound.
Pirate treasure is direct; ocean only via sunken treasure.
Ocean waves are direct; no pirate link.

pairs.pairNote: REEF is the clean compound; the rest point at one side with a nod to the other.

clues.revealExplanation: Reef sharks on the ocean reef.

blindReview.reason: Reefs are ocean features and reef shark is a familiar compound.
The deep is the ocean; shark only as a deep-sea creature.

provenance.authorReason: colour; blue shark is a stretch

blindReview.reason: Blue ocean is direct; the blue shark species is a secondary link.

clues.wordAConnection: Jaws is set on the ocean.

clues.revealExplanation: A metal robot; heavy metal rock.

blindReview.reason: Robots are metal; rock only via heavy metal as a rock genre or metal ore in rock.

clues.wordAConnection: Doing the robot on the dance floor.
clues.revealExplanation: The robot dance; rock music to dance to.

blindReview.reason: The Robot is a dance; rock reaches dance only as music you dance to.

Robots are steel; steel is not rock.

provenance.authorReason: rock and roll reaches ROCK only

blindReview.reason: Rock and roll is direct; nothing rolls about a robot.

pairs.pairNote: SKIP is the one hint that names the shared activity.

clues.revealExplanation: Skipping rocks on the water.

Water pool is direct; rock pool is the British term where Americans say tide pool.

clues.wordBConnection: Spring is when it comes back.

pairs.pairNote: STEAM is a strong single bridge; the other two are one-sided.

clues.revealExplanation: A steam train: water boiled into steam.

blindReview.reason: Steam train, and steam is heated water.
